title: Bird on a Plum Branch
medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper

altText: A Japanese woodblock print of a small bird perched on a branch of a plum tree. The bird and the branch are shown in clear outlines with flat areas of color on paper.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, period (Edo period, 1615–1868; the object date field is blank), medium, public-domain flag, credit line, culture (Japan), tags (Birds, Trees), and image URLs read from the record

context: A woodblock print by Utagawa Hiroshige (1797 to 1858), the Japanese artist best known for landscapes. The Met's record does not give an exact year, only the Edo period, which ran from 1615 to 1868. Pictures of birds and flowering branches were a popular subject in Japanese prints.

descriptions.k: A little bird sits on a branch. The branch is from a plum tree. Plum trees have flowers in early spring. Can you find the bird? Look at its tiny feet holding on. What do you think it will do next?
descriptions.g12: Hiroshige made this print in Japan long ago. A small bird sits on a branch of a plum tree. Plum trees bloom early in spring, so the picture may feel like the end of winter. Prints like this are made with carved wood blocks. How do the bird and branch fit the paper? What season does it feel like?
descriptions.g35: Utagawa Hiroshige is best known for landscapes, but he also made prints of birds and flowers like this one. A small bird perches on a plum branch, and plum trees bloom early in the year. The picture was printed from carved wood blocks, with color added block by block. Look at how the bird and branch are placed on the paper. What makes this simple scene feel peaceful?
descriptions.g68: Hiroshige, who lived from 1797 to 1858, made many bird-and-flower prints in addition to his famous landscapes. In this woodblock print a small bird perches on a plum branch, a subject linked in Japan to the first signs of spring. The Met dates it only to the Edo period. Notice how clear outlines and flat areas of color make the composition simple and elegant. How does the artist use the shape of the paper to place the branch?
descriptions.g910: Bird on a Plum Branch shows how Hiroshige, famous for landscapes, applied the clarity of woodblock printing to a small natural subject. The plum, which blooms early in the year, is often connected in East Asian art with the arrival of spring, and a bird adds life to the branch. Outline, flat color, and careful placement on the sheet give the print economy and grace. Consider how a printed image can feel both intimate and designed.
descriptions.g1112: Hiroshige's bird-and-flower prints extend the ukiyo-e tradition beyond landscape and city life, drawing on a long East Asian pairing of birds with seasonal plants. The plum blossom's association with early spring invites seasonal and poetic readings, though the Met's record gives no accompanying text or exact date to anchor one. The woodblock process, with its division of labor among artist, carver, and printer, also shapes how we interpret authorship. What can the composition and technique support, and what remains uncertain?

teacherNote.context: A woodblock print by Utagawa Hiroshige of a bird on a plum branch. The Met's record gives only the Edo period (1615 to 1868), not an exact year.
directions: Have students make a simple stamp print of a bird using a potato or foam block, then discuss what is lost and gained compared with drawing.
Discuss how the empty space in the print affects what viewers notice.
Compare this quiet image with the busier city scenes in the archive.
